title: Bradyarrhythmias, Conduction Disease and Cardiac Pacing

steps.tx: **Sick sinus syndrome** encompasses sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest, sinoatrial exit block, and tachycardia-bradycardia syndrome, where symptomatic **chronotropic incompetence** is a primary indication for permanent pacing. Inability to increase heart rate appropriately with physical exertion produces severe fatigue, presyncope, and exertional dyspnea. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

steps.tx: **Mobitz type I** **Wenckebach** second-degree AV block exhibits progressive PR interval prolongation ending in a non-conducted P wave, localizing within the atrioventricular node in over 70% of cases, typically carrying a benign prognosis. Type **1** block often improves with exercise or atropine.

steps.tx: **Mobitz type II** second-degree AV block is characterized by constant PR intervals before unexpected non-conducted P waves, almost invariably localizing to the **infranodal** His-Purkinje system, carrying high risk of progression to complete heart block. Type **2** block represents a Class I pacemaker indication.

steps.tx: Third-degree or **complete AV block** demonstrates complete **atrioventricular dissociation** where atrial rate exceeds ventricular rate, requiring permanent pacemaker implantation to prevent fatal asystolic pauses. Advanced block originating in infranodal tissue produces an unstable wide-complex escape rhythm at **3**0 beats per minute. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

Advanced block originating in infranodal tissue produces an unstable wide-complex escape rhythm at 30 beats per minute. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

rows: Unstable; prone to syncope and arrest

steps.tx: Tracing shows independent P waves marching through at near eighty five while broad QRS beats escape near thirty with no link between them. That **dissociation** defines complete **block** where atria and ventricles beat alone. Spotting the slow wide **escape** matters because infranodal origin is unstable and needs prompt permanent pacing to avert pause.
steps.say: The ECG shows regular P waves marching independently of slow wide QRS complexes with different atrial and ventricular rates. That separation means complete atrioventricular dissociation with a ventricular escape rhythm. The wide slow escape signals an infranodal source that is fragile. In the lesson this finding calls for permanent pacing to prevent syncope or arrest.

steps.tx: **Physiological pacing** via **conduction system pacing** utilizes **His bundle pacing** or left bundle branch area pacing to preserve normal ventricular activation sequence and prevent pacing-induced cardiomyopathy. Direct capture of the specialized His-Purkinje system maintains narrow physiological QRS complexes and synchronous ventricular contraction.

Direct capture of the specialized His-Purkinje system maintains narrow physiological QRS complexes and synchronous ventricular contraction.

left.title: Conduction System Pacing (CSP)
points: Preserves normal narrow physiological QRS complex
Prevents pacing-induced cardiomyopathy in RV-dependent pacing

right.title: Right Ventricular Apical Pacing
points: Produces broad, abnormal LBBB-like QRS complex
Leads to left ventricular adverse remodeling over time
Associated with increased heart failure and AF incidence

steps.tx: **Pacemaker syndrome** occurs during single-chamber ventricular pacing when ventricular contraction occurs without preceding atrial systole, causing retrograde ventriculoatrial conduction, **cannon A waves**, fatigue, and hypotension, which resolves upon upgrading to dual-chamber pacing. Atrial contraction against closed AV valves causes jugular pulsation. Comprehensive clinical evaluation requires careful correlation with serial electrocardiographic tracings and hemodynamic parameters.

steps.tx: **Leadless pacemakers** including **Micra** and Aveir are self-contained intracardiac capsules deployed transcatheterly into the right ventricle, eliminating pocket infections, lead fractures, and vascular occlusions. Transcatheter delivery through the femoral vein significantly reduces long-term lead-related infections, preserving central venous patency and avoiding upper extremity vascular complications.

steps.tx: The cutaway shows a **leadless pacemaker** capsule anchored in the **right ventricle** by nitinol fixation tines gripping the trabeculae. The inset traces its **transcatheter** delivery from the femoral vein up through the **inferior vena cava**. With no pocket and no leads, this design avoids pocket infection, lead fracture and venous occlusion. It suits patients needing single chamber ventricular pacing.
steps.say: A leadless pacemaker is a self contained capsule fixed directly inside the right ventricle. Small tines anchor it into the muscle wall, and it arrives through a catheter passed up the femoral vein and inferior vena cava. Because there is no chest pocket and no thin lead running through veins, pocket infection and lead fracture are avoided. It provides single chamber pacing from within the heart.

vis.caption: Leadless pacemaker anchored in the right ventricle after femoral delivery, Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Trifascicular block** on ECG is defined by complete RBBB with left anterior or posterior fascicular block and **alternating bundle branch block** or first-degree AV block, carrying a high risk of sudden progression to complete AV block. Alternating bundle branch block represents a Class **1** indication for permanent pacemaker implantation.
